A ball’s ultimate chance of being ejected depends on the position in which it first appears.

• If a ball first enters in position 3, its ejection probability is 17⁄27 ≈ 0.6296.
• If it first enters in position 2, its ejection probability is 5⁄9 ≈ 0.5556.
• No ball ever first enters in position 1.

Ball 3 is the only ball guaranteed to start in position 3 (the initial layout is 1-2-3). Every later ball can start in position 2 or 3, so its overall ejection chance is at most 17⁄27 and usually lower. Therefore the highest attainable winning probability belongs uniquely to ball 3.
A ball’s chance to be ejected depends only on the position it first occupies on the three-ball platform.

Let p₁, p₂, p₃ be the probabilities that a ball eventually gets ejected (instead of merely rolling away) if it first appears in positions 1, 2, 3 respectively.

1. Position 1: it is ejected only if piston 1 fires before pistons 2 or 3 do.
   p₁ = 1⁄3.

2. Position 2: with probability 1⁄3 it is ejected immediately (piston 2 fires); with probability 2⁄3 it moves to position 1, after which its chance is p₁.
   p₂ = 1⁄3 + (2⁄3)·p₁ = 1⁄3 + 2⁄9 = 5⁄9.

3. Position 3: with probability 1⁄3 it is ejected immediately (piston 3 fires); with probability 1⁄3 it moves to position 1 (via piston 2) and with probability 1⁄3 it moves to position 2 (via piston 1).
   p₃ = 1⁄3 + (1⁄3)·p₁ + (1⁄3)·p₂ = 1⁄3 + 1⁄9 + 5⁄27 = 17⁄27 ≈ 0.63.

Only balls 1 and 2 ever start in positions 1 and 2; every other ball (starting with ball 3) first appears in position 3 and so enjoys the highest probability 17⁄27.

To maximize your winning odds you should therefore pick the earliest ball that enters in position 3, namely ball number 3.

If at least one human lived in the village, the sentence “At least one of us is a human” would be true. Humans may utter true statements, but vampires must not. Therefore any vampire present could not truthfully say that sentence. Because every resident gives that same sentence, its truth-value must be the same for each speaker.

Two consistent possibilities exist:
1. All 100 are humans – sentence true, everyone truthful.
2. All 100 are vampires – sentence false, everyone lying.

You have already seen a vampire the previous night, so the first possibility is impossible. Hence every resident is a vampire.
Let H be the number of humans and V the number of vampires (H+V = 100).
All 100 residents give exactly the same sentence: “At least one of us is a human.”
1. If H ≥ 1 and V ≥ 1, the sentence is TRUE (since there is a human). Humans could say it, but vampires cannot, because they must lie; thus mixed populations are impossible.
2. If H = 100 (V = 0), the sentence is TRUE and every resident (all humans) can utter it; this fits truth-telling but contradicts the fact that you actually saw a vampire the previous night, so V ≠ 0.
3. Therefore H must be 0 and V = 100. In that case the sentence “At least one of us is a human” is FALSE, and every resident (all vampires) lies by stating it. This matches both their lying nature and your observation of a vampire.
Hence all 100 villagers are vampires.

Let Bob use the same guess g for every box.  
Payoff = g·k, where k is the number of boxes that contain at least g coins.  

Host’s goal is to minimize g·k subject to the constraints on the coin distribution.

1.  For g ≥ 13 the host can pick a distribution whose largest box has ≤ 12 coins (e.g. (12,12,6)), so k = 0 and Bob wins nothing.  Hence Bob must choose g ≤ 12.

2.  For 7 ≤ g ≤ 12 the host can make exactly one box reach g (e.g. (13,7,10) for g = 12), giving k = 1, so Bob’s worst-case payoff is g.

3.  For 1 ≤ g ≤ 6 the host must have at least two boxes ≥ g (e.g. (24,6,0)), so k = 2 and the worst-case payoff is 2g.

Therefore the maximum of the worst-case payoffs is
max{2g : 1≤g≤6} ∪ {g : 7≤g≤12} = max{12,12} = 12 coins.

Thus Bob can guarantee at least 12 coins, and each coin is worth $1 000.
Let Bob’s three guesses, arranged in non-decreasing order, be g₁ ≤ g₂ ≤ g₃.

Take the host’s distribution (0, 6, 24); it satisfies all the constraints (one box has at least 2 coins and one box has 6 more coins than another).  After Bob announces his guesses, the host is free to match them with the boxes in whatever way is worst for Bob.

• The host will pair the largest guess g₃ with the 0-coin box.  If g₃ > 0, Bob earns 0 from that box.

• The host next pairs the second-largest guess g₂ with the 6-coin box.  If g₂ > 6, Bob again earns 0; if g₂ ≤ 6, Bob earns g₂.

• The remaining guess g₁ is matched with the 24-coin box, so Bob earns g₁ (provided g₁ ≤ 24, which is always true if g₁ ≤ g₂ ≤ g₃). 

Hence Bob’s total guarantee against this single distribution is
  0 + 0 + g₁    if g₂ > 6,
  g₂ + g₁         if g₂ ≤ 6.

To maximise the worst-case total he therefore wants g₂ ≤ 6, and within that restriction he wants g₁ and g₂ as large as possible.  Since g₁ ≤ g₂ ≤ 6, the best he can do is choose
  g₁ = 6, g₂ = 6.
(Any choice for g₃ ≥ 6 gives the same guarantee, so set g₃ = 6 as well.)

With the guess triple (6, 6, 6) Bob is guaranteed at least
  6 + 6 = 12 coins
against the distribution (0, 6, 24).  No strategy can guarantee more than 12 coins, because the argument above shows that any guesses give at most 12 coins versus that same distribution.

Therefore the maximum amount Bob can force himself to win is 12 coins, and since each coin is worth $1 000, the minimum amount of money he can be certain of winning is
 12 × $1 000 = $12 000.
